column5: treasured possession; mercy on the day
column6: The commentary calls the day owner both merciful and the one to whom all finally belong; Malachi says that on the day he acts, YHWH will make those who fear him his treasured possession and spare them as a father spares a serving son.

column5: Day of YHWH; wrath against sinners
column6: The commentary calls the day an arriving event rather than a calendar date; Isaiah announces the coming Day of YHWH as a day of wrath that makes the land desolate and destroys its sinners.

column5: source yawm; Hebrew yom; approaching bitter day
column6: The commentary gives yawm the force of an approaching overwhelming event; cognate Hebrew yom in Zephaniah's Day of YHWH is near, bitter, and marked by the warrior's cry rather than ordinary solar routine.

column5: dead arise from dust
column6: The commentary's day makes those who have died arrive for final accounting; Isaiah speaks of the dead living, corpses rising, and those in the dust awakening.

column5: owner requires flock from shepherds
column6: The commentary makes leading a flock a form of responsible possession; Ezekiel has God oppose the self-feeding shepherds, require his sheep from their hand, and reclaim the flock.

column5: judgment between sheep, rams, and goats
column6: The commentary turns flock imagery into a day of differentiation and account; Ezekiel explicitly says God judges between sheep and sheep, rams and goats.

column5: leaders mislead; followers destroyed
column6: The commentary contrasts the true caller who leads straight with Pharaoh's fatal leadership; Isaiah says a people's leaders make them err and those led by them are swallowed up.

column5: YHWH at the head of a people going out
column6: The commentary's guide is the one who goes before and determines the route; Micah's restoration procession has its king pass before the people with YHWH at their head.

column5: blind guides and the pit
column6: The commentary's false front-runner brings followers to fire instead of water; Jesus calls false leaders blind guides and says guide and follower alike fall into a pit.

column5: hour of judgment; worship of Creator
column6: The commentary joins sole ownership, the coming day, and worship; Revelation's angel announces that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls all to worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs.

column5: coming with recompense for each work
column6: The commentary defines dîn as exact return for what each person has done; the coming speaker in Revelation brings recompense to repay each according to work.

column5: repayment to each according to works
column6: The commentary makes final repayment individual and proportionate; Paul states the same judicial rule in saying that God renders to each person according to works.

column5: all exposed before the one to whom account is due
column6: The commentary says the hidden interior reaches the account after human witnesses stop; Hebrews says no creature is hidden and all are naked and exposed before the one to whom account must be given.

column5: death once, then judgment
column6: The commentary uses the deathbed to show that a person cannot recover the life already claimed; Hebrews sets death once for humans and judgment afterward.

column5: bring nothing in; take nothing out
column6: The commentary says possessions, servants, and status are left behind when the person comes alone; Paul states the compact formula that nothing was brought into the world and nothing can be taken out.

column5: liturgical petition to forgive debts
column6: The commentary moves from naming the owner to direct address and treats debt forgiveness as the measure of hoped-for mercy; the Lord's Prayer asks the Father to forgive debts as petitioners forgive their debtors.

column5: postmortem reversal of comfort and anguish
column6: The commentary's denied water scene is a recompense in which prior possession no longer helps; Abraham explains the rich man's torment and Lazarus's comfort as a reversal of their former received portions.

column5: withheld wages cry to the Lord
column6: The commentary binds denial of the poor's due to the day of account; James says unpaid wages cry out and the cries of harvesters reach the Lord of hosts.

column5: Christ titled King of kings and Lord of lords
column6: The commentary concentrates final kingship in the one divine owner of the day; Revelation gives the victorious Christ the title King of kings and Lord of lords, a specifically Christian royal identification.

column5: borrower servant to lender
column6: The commentary links debt's due date to ownership and servitude; Proverbs states the social analogy directly by making the borrower servant to the lender.

column5: God weighs heart and repays work
column6: The commentary's unbending scale reaches the heart as well as outward deeds; Proverbs asks whether the one who weighs the heart does not know and then says he repays each according to work.

column5: weighed in a just balance
column6: The commentary turns the day into a balance that cannot bend for wealth or status; Job asks to be weighed in just scales so that God may know his integrity.

column5: YHWH enters judgment with fire
column6: The commentary describes the day as an event that arrives with fire and judgment; Isaiah presents YHWH entering judgment with fire and sword against all flesh.

column5: Lord Jesus revealed in flaming fire
column6: The commentary names the single owner as the judge of the fire-bound day; 2 Thessalonians presents the revealed Lord Jesus in flaming fire as the one inflicting retribution, a Christian specification of the judging figure.

column5: death, resurrection, judgment, royal reckoning
column6: The commentary treats death, return, and accounting as one continuous claim of the day owner; Avot's maxim makes those born die, the dead live, and the living stand for judgment before the King of kings.

column5: faithful commerce questioned at judgment
column6: The commentary uses debt writing and commercial honesty to show that ordinary accounts continue before God; this talmudic judgment scene begins by asking whether a person conducted business faithfully.

column5: one mediator between God and humans
column6: The commentary limits effective intercession to the owner's authorization; 1 Timothy states a Christian mediatorial formula that names one God and one mediator, the human Christ Jesus.

column5: throne before which earth and sky flee
column6: The commentary's day has the earth grasped and the heavens folded beneath sovereign rule; at Revelation's great white throne, earth and sky flee from the judge's presence.

column5: resurrection without marriage
column6: The commentary uses spouse and family bonds to show relations that cannot carry another person through the day; Jesus recasts the resurrection state as one in which people neither marry nor are given in marriage.

column5: judgment has its appointed time
column6: The commentary calls the owned day the time when all accounts close; Qohelet says God judges righteous and wicked because there is a time for every matter and every work.

column5: measure returned in judgment
column6: The commentary describes dîn as a counterweight that returns what a person has done; Jesus says the measure used for others will be measured back to the user.

column5: sowing and reaping
column6: The commentary sees final recompense as the completion of habitual conduct rather than an isolated act; Paul says no one mocks God because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
